1205.title: Greed and generosity
1205.howItsDone: Christians practice generosity through tithes and offerings to their church, alms for the poor, and private giving; Christian teaching on the deadly sins pairs greed, or avarice, with generosity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, acedia, the noonday demon: the monks' heavy boredom with good things. Your line was the noonday demon.

Every morning in the wilderness, bread is lying on the ground. The Israelites call it manna. The instruction is simple: gather what you need for today, and keep none till morning. Some of them keep some anyway. Just in case. And the next morning, "it bred worms, and stank." The bread that fed them, stored up, went bad overnight. And the ones who gathered a lot? The text says they had nothing left over. The ones who gathered a little had enough.

Greed is a closed hand. It gathers, and then it grips. Often it's less about wanting more things than about fear: what if there isn't enough tomorrow? The manna story answers that fear strangely. The hoard doesn't protect you; the daily gathering does. Jesus says it plainly in Luke: "Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth." Your life isn't the pile. For the opposite, the Bible uses hands. In Deuteronomy, the law turns to the poor among the people: don't "shut thine hand from thy poor brother," but "thou shalt open thine hand wide." Not a little. Wide. Much later, Paul goes back to the manna. He's collecting money for a poor church in Jerusalem, and he quotes the old story: "He that had gathered much had nothing over; and he that had gathered little had no lack." For Paul, the manna pictures sharing: what one has too much of, another needs, and generosity evens it out. He adds one more thing: "God loveth a cheerful giver." Not dutiful, not guilty. Gladly, without counting first. So generosity is less about the size of a gift than the shape of the hand. A closed hand can hold on to a lot, but it can't receive anything either. An open hand can let go, and it's ready to be filled. Christians practice this through tithes, offerings, alms, or quiet gifts nobody sees. The shape is the same.

Picture your shelves, your closet, your calendar, and let one thing come to mind you could give that you hadn't planned to: some money, a coat you don't wear, an hour, a meal for someone. Don't weigh it too long. If you pray, you can offer it with Paul's phrase: a cheerful giver.
Greed and generosity. The closed hand that hoards out of fear, and the open hand that lets go and can be filled.
Your line: open hands. Like the manna, enough for today really can be enough. Until tomorrow.

1206.title: Gluttony and temperance
1206.hook: too much, too fast, too fussy
1206.howItsDone: Some Christians say grace before meals, some with a set prayer and some in their own words, and some churches keep fasting days; Christian teaching on the deadly sins pairs gluttony with temperance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, greed and generosity: manna that went bad overnight, and the open hand. Your line was open hands.

Esau comes in from the field, starving. His brother Jacob has a pot of red lentil stew on the fire. Esau doesn't even name the dish: "Feed me, I pray thee, with that same red pottage; for I am faint." Jacob names a price: your birthright, the eldest son's inheritance. And Esau, in the moment, can only see the bowl. He swears, he eats, he drinks, he gets up and goes. The text ends it with one flat line: "thus Esau despised his birthright." A whole future, for one meal, right now.

Gluttony sounds like a sin about eating too much, and that's part of it. But some Christian teachers saw more than size in it. Gregory the Great, a pope and teacher, listed the ways a person can go wrong at the table, and only one of them is quantity. Eating too soon, before the time. Too lavishly, always needing the expensive thing. Too much. Too eagerly, wolfing it down. And too fussily, where it all has to be just so. Each one makes food the center of the world. That's what happened to Esau. Hunger is not a sin; he really was faint. But in that moment the bowl got bigger than his family, his future, his promise. The letter to the Hebrews remembers him exactly that way, as the one "who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright." So what's the opposite? Christian tradition calls it temperance, and it isn't joyless. When Jesus fed the crowd on the hillside, the Gospel slows down before anyone eats: he took the loaves and the fishes, and "looking up to heaven, he blessed, and brake." The answer to gluttony is less about eating less than about receiving food differently. Paul widens it: "whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God." That's one reason some Christians begin a meal with a pause, a grace: a set prayer, a few words of their own, or a bowed head for one breath. The pause puts the bowl back in its place: a gift, not a master.

Bring to mind your next meal and decide on a small pause at the start: a breath, a few words of thanks, a thought for who grew it, cooked it, carried it. If you pray, you can say a grace you already know. Then picture the first few bites, slow enough to taste.
Gluttony and temperance. Letting food become the center, too much, too fast or too fussy; and receiving it as a good gift, with thanks.
Your line: eat with thanks. Hunger is no sin; the bowl just isn't the world. Rest well.

1207.title: Lust and chastity
1207.hook: chastity means love that respects people, whether single or married
1207.tomorrow: works of mercy for the body
1207.howItsDone: Christian churches teach chastity as a virtue for everyone: for single people as abstaining from sex outside marriage, and for married people as faithfulness to one spouse; Christian teaching on the deadly sins pairs lust with chastity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gluttony and temperance: Esau and the red stew. Your line was eat with thanks.

Evening in Jerusalem, in the season when kings go out to battle. But King David has stayed home. He gets up from his bed and walks on the palace roof, and from there he sees a woman bathing, "and the woman was very beautiful to look upon." The next words are quiet and terrible: "David sent and enquired after the woman." He learns her name, Bathsheba. He learns she is married, to one of his own soldiers, away at the war. And he sends for her anyway. A look, then a question, then a summons.

Notice how the story moves. David doesn't start with a crime. He starts with a look, and the look becomes a plan, and the plan treats Bathsheba as something a king can send for. In the whole scene she barely speaks. She is acted upon. That's the heart of what Christian teaching means by lust. Not desire itself: the Bible celebrates desire, and gives a whole book, the Song of Songs, to lovers longing for each other. Lust is desire that turns a person into a thing to be used. Jesus takes it inward, to the look: "whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart." Chastity is the answer, and it's more than a no. In Christian teaching it's for everyone: for someone single, churches teach it as waiting; for someone married, as faithfulness to one person. Either way, the root is love that respects the whole person. Why the whole person? Because of the Bible's first page: "God created man in his own image." In Christian teaching, every person you see carries that image. And Paul tells the Corinthians, "your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost." Not a thing. A temple. Christians differ on many questions about sex and marriage, and churches teach different things on some of them. But the lines from Genesis and from Paul point one way: a person is never an object. And David's story doesn't end on the roof. The prophet Nathan comes to him later, and David hears what he's done.

Bring to mind a few people you'll see or scroll past today, a coworker, a stranger on the street, someone on a screen, and for each one slowly add what you can't see: a mother somewhere, a bad night, a favorite song, a name. Let each one become a whole life, not a picture. If you pray, you can hold Genesis in mind: made in the image of God.
Lust and chastity. Desire that uses a person, and love that respects the whole person, whether single or married.
Your line: people, not things. In Christian teaching, every face carries that image. See you soon.

1208.title: Works of mercy for the body
1208.word: Works of mercy for the body
1208.hook: feed, give drink, clothe, shelter, visit the sick and prisoners, bury the dead
1208.tomorrow: works of mercy for the soul
1208.howItsDone: Christians practice the works of mercy for the body, often called the corporal works of mercy, through food banks, shelters, hospital and prison visiting, and funeral ministries, and in ordinary help to neighbors; the list comes from Matthew 25 with burial of the dead from Tobit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, lust and chastity: David on the roof, and the whole person. Your line was people, not things.

The table is set for a feast. A man named Tobit is about to eat, and he sends his son out to find a poor man to share the meal. The son comes back with news instead: a man of their people has been killed, and his body is lying in the marketplace. Tobit gets up before he has tasted anything. He carries the body to a room and waits for sunset to bury it. His neighbors laugh at him. Burying the dead has already got him into trouble with the king. He does it anyway. His dinner, the book says, he ate in sorrow.

Tobit's book sits in the Bibles of Catholic and Orthodox Christians; Protestant Bibles that print it place it among the books called the Apocrypha. Either way, tradition says his story gave Christians one item on an old list: the works of mercy for the body. The rest comes straight from Jesus. In Matthew's Gospel he tells a story of the end of all things. The nations are gathered, and the king says to some of them: "For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in: Naked, and ye clothed me: I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me." Add Tobit's burial to those, and that's the list the tradition hands on. Then the story turns. The people the king praises don't know what he means: "Lord, when saw we thee an hungred, and fed thee?" They never noticed. They were just feeding people. And the king answers: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." In this story, the hungry stranger and Christ are somehow the same face. So these works aren't charity from a distance. They are hands: a plate, a cup, a coat, a chair beside a hospital bed, a visit through a glass window, a shovel at a grave. Some Christians trace hospitals, soup kitchens and prison visiting back to these verses. But the works can stay small: one meal brought to one neighbor.
screen: `I WAS AN HUNGRED, AND YE GAVE.`

segments.voice: Let the king's list pass by slowly, the hungry, the thirsty, the cold, the homeless, the sick, the locked away, the grieving, until one face rises, and one small thing your hands could do for them: a meal, a call, a visit. If you pray, you can hold that person before God.
Works of mercy for the body. Feed the hungry, give drink, clothe, shelter, visit the sick and prisoners, bury the dead.

1209.title: Works of mercy for the soul
1209.word: Works of mercy for the soul
1209.hook: teach, counsel, correct gently, comfort, forgive, bear wrongs, pray
1209.howItsDone: Christians practice the works of mercy for the soul, often called the spiritual works of mercy, through teaching, counseling, comforting the grieving, forgiving and praying for others; Catholic and Orthodox Christians include prayer for the dead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tobit's burial, and the least of these. Your line was mercy with hands.

Job has lost nearly everything: his children, his wealth, his health. He sits in the ashes. Three friends travel to see him, and when they arrive they barely recognize him. They weep, they tear their robes, and then they do something remarkable: "they sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great." A week of silence, side by side in the dirt. It may be the best thing they ever did for him. Because then the talking started.

Christian tradition keeps a second list of mercy, for the heart and mind, and each item is done with words, or with holding words back. Teach someone who doesn't know. Counsel someone who doubts. Correct someone gently. Comfort the sorrowful. Forgive. Bear wrongs patiently. Pray for others. Correcting comes with a warning label. Paul writes, "if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted." Restore, not crush; you could be next. Comfort, in Paul, travels in a circle: God "comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble." Now back to Job. After the silence, Job speaks first, cursing the day he was born. Then his friends answer, and for chapter after chapter they explain his suffering to him. You must have done something. Confess it. God is punishing you. They meant to counsel and correct. But at the end of the book God says to one of them, "ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath." That's the warning built into these works: the same sentence can heal or wound. The friends were best when they were silent and present, so the tradition pairs these works with patience and humility. On the last item, churches differ: Catholic and Orthodox Christians pray for the living and the dead; Protestant churches have taught differently about prayer for the dead, and differ among themselves. Prayer for the living is shared.

Ask yourself the list as questions, who needs teaching, comfort, gentle correction, forgiveness, prayer, and when one person rises, sit with them in silence for a while, the way Job's friends did at first. If you pray, you can pray for them now. And if the grief is your own and it has gotten very dark, in the US you can call or text 988, or reach local emergency help.
Works of mercy for the soul. Teach, counsel, correct gently, comfort, forgive, bear wrongs, and pray for others.

1210.title: Conscience
1210.hook: the inner voice, formed by prayer and learning, to be followed
1210.howItsDone: Christians form conscience through prayer, scripture, the teaching of their church and the counsel of others, and some examine their conscience at the end of the day or before confession or communion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, works of mercy for the soul: Job's friends, silent and then too sure. Your line was mercy with words.

A cave in the wilderness. In the dark at the back, David and his men are hiding from King Saul, who has come with an army to kill him. Then Saul himself walks into the very same cave, alone, with no idea who's in there. David's men whisper: this is the day. God has handed him to you. David creeps forward in the dark and quietly cuts a corner off the king's robe. That's all. Then he goes back. And the text says: "David's heart smote him, because he had cut off Saul's skirt." Not for killing him. For a piece of cloth.

Something in David spoke up, and over something small. His men saw a chance. His conscience saw the king. David tells his men he will not lift his hand against "the LORD's anointed," and he holds them back. Christians call that inner voice conscience, and Paul writes about it. He describes people who never had the law of Moses but still know right from wrong, the work of the law "written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness." A witness inside, sometimes accusing, sometimes excusing. Then a caution: Christian teaching says conscience has to be formed. It isn't automatically right. It can be dulled by habit, made too harsh, or trained by a crowd. Paul spends whole chapters on believers whose consciences disagree about what's allowed, and asks them to be patient with each other. So Christians tend a conscience the way you tend a garden: with prayer, scripture, the teaching of their church, and honest friends. A psalm puts the prayer side simply: "Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts." And once it's formed, conscience is to be followed. Paul tells a Roman governor, in Acts, that he works "to have always a conscience void of offence toward God, and toward men." Churches speak of this in their own ways. Catholic teaching calls conscience a judgment a person must obey, and must also form. Some Protestant teachers speak of a conscience bound to scripture. In both, it's the place where a person stands alone before God.

Let the last day or two pass slowly through your mind, a conversation, an email, a choice, and see if there's a small place where something tugged, the way David's heart smote him over a corner of cloth. Don't argue with it yet, and don't punish yourself; just listen. If you pray, you can borrow the psalm: search me, O God, and know my heart.
Conscience. The inner witness that knows right from wrong, formed by prayer and learning, and then followed.
Your line: the inner voice. Formed first, with care, and then followed. See you tomorrow.

1211.title: Just war
1211.hook: Augustine and Aquinas set limits on war: just cause, last resort, protect civilians
1211.howItsDone: Catholic teaching and some Protestant and Orthodox thinkers use just war criteria to judge when force may be used and how it must be limited, while the historic peace churches reject war altogether; some churches include prayers for those in authority in their services.

segments.voice: Yesterday, conscience: David in the cave, and a corner of cloth. Your line was the inner voice.

Crowds have come out to the Jordan River to hear John the Baptist, and he's not gentle with them. Group after group asks the same thing: what shall we do? Then some soldiers step forward, men who carry swords for a living, under Roman rule. John answers: "Do violence to no man, neither accuse any falsely; and be content with your wages." He doesn't tell them to put down the sword. He doesn't bless whatever they do with it either. He draws lines around it.

War is a hard subject in the Bible itself. The prophet Isaiah longed for the day when "they shall beat their swords into plowshares," and "nation shall not lift up sword against nation." In the garden, when one of his followers drew a sword, Jesus said that "all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword." And yet nations go to war, and Christians live in those nations, serve in their armies, and lead some of them. So some Christian teachers asked: if war comes, can it ever be right, and under what limits? Augustine, a bishop in North Africa, wrote to a Roman general about how a soldier could please God. War, he answered, may only be waged for the sake of peace, never for its own sake. Elsewhere he named what makes war evil: love of cruelty, and a lust for power. Much later Thomas Aquinas set conditions: it must be declared by a rightful authority, for a just cause, and with a right intention, aiming at good and away from evil. Later teachers added that war must be a last resort, and that people who aren't fighting must be protected. Together these became just war teaching. Notice what it is and isn't. It isn't a cheer for war. It's a fence around it: its rules are reasons not to fight, or limits on how to fight. Not every Christian accepts it; tomorrow, churches that refuse war altogether. And looking back over this week: open hands, eating with thanks, people not things, mercy with hands, mercy with words, the inner voice, and now limits on war itself.

Bring to mind a place where people are fighting, or a leader deciding whether they will, and the people far away who will live with that choice. The first letter to Timothy asks for prayers "for kings, and for all that are in authority": if you pray, you can do that now; if not, simply hold them, and the people under them, in your attention.
Just war. Christian teaching that sets limits on war: a just cause, rightful authority, right intention, last resort, and protection for those not fighting.
Your line: war has limits. Even there, the people who aren't fighting count. Until tomorrow.

fork.setup: you're a soldier at the Jordan. you've heard John tell the crowds to share their coats and food. you ask him, "and what shall we do?" what does he say?
options: lay down your swords and go home.
do violence to no man, accuse no one falsely, be content with your wages.
fight for Israel against Rome.
fork.reveal: John draws lines around a soldier's work: no violence, no false accusations, no grabbing for more. Christians read his answer in different ways.

original.note: Latin: just war, the name used for this teaching.

trapdoor: what you thought: just war means Christians think war is fine.
what it means: limits on war: only for peace, with rightful authority, a just cause, right intention, as a last resort, sparing those not fighting.
what a scholar hears: Augustine's letter to a Roman general, Aquinas's conditions in the Summa, and later teachers adding last resort and civilian protection.
guess: teaching that sets strict limits on any war
the belief that any war for your country is right
a war fought only with fair, equal weapons

chat.says: So does just war teaching mean Christians think war is a good thing?
options: No. It's a fence, not a cheer: a just cause, a last resort, protecting people not fighting.
Yes. It says that any war a nation declares is blessed, as long as it wins.
Sort of. It only limits how wars end, not when or why they're allowed to start.
chat.meaning: Just war teaching is a fence around war, not a cheer: rightful authority, a just cause, right intention, last resort, and protection for people not fighting.

John the Baptist.meaning: a prophet who preached to the crowds at the Jordan River

plowshares.meaning: the blades of a plow, for farming

Augustine.meaning: a bishop in North Africa and early Christian teacher

Thomas Aquinas.meaning: a medieval teacher who set conditions on war

Timothy.meaning: a young church leader; two New Testament letters bear his name

sources.ref: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II q.40 a.1
